chain: Antioxidant pill with vitamins A, C, E
procyanidin-oral-melasma.text: Users take oral procyanidin with vitamins A, C and E to fade melasma patches and even out facial skin tone from the inside. It has been tested in one small 8-week placebo-controlled trial in women with epidermal melasma; larger studies have not been reported.

quinine-skin-lightener.text: Quinine has turned up as an ingredient in illicit skin-lightening products sold for a paler complexion, alongside steroids and mercury compounds. Its use for skin tone is based on product reports and enforcement records; it has not been studied as a lightener.

lead-based-ceruse.text: Ceruse was a white face paste used for centuries to give a pale, even complexion and cover blemishes, scars and freckles. The whitening was immediately visible, and pale skin signalled wealth and leisure. It is documented as a historical cosmetic rather than a modern option.

pearl-extract.text: Pearl extract and powder are used in traditional Chinese medicine and in cosmetics marketed for brightening and anti-aging. Appearance claims rest on a long tradition and mostly laboratory-level findings, with few human skin trials.

fermented-rice-water-sake-lees.text: Sake lees is used in J-beauty masks, creams and bath powders for a brighter, moisturized complexion. Users report a glow after use, and laboratory work has found tyrosinase-inhibiting activity; controlled human trials of its brightening effect are limited.

citric-acid.text: Citric acid appears in cosmetics as a pH adjuster and in some chemical peels as an alpha hydroxy acid for smoother, brighter skin. Its exfoliating use is common in formulations, while skin-specific trials of citric acid itself are scarce.

chain: Old skin sheds, new skin forms
trichloroacetic-acid-peel.text: TCA peels are done in clinics to improve sun-damaged skin, melasma, acne marks and scars, giving a fresher, more even surface after healing. Small clinical trials have studied these uses, particularly photodamage, melasma and acne.

lactobionic-acid.text: Lactobionic acid is sold as a gentle polyhydroxy acid in skincare, used for smoother, hydrated skin with less stinging than stronger acids. Its chemistry and use in organ-transplant solutions are well documented; published skin trials are few.

chain: Dead cells loosen with low irritation
gluconolactone.text: Gluconolactone is a polyhydroxy acid in skincare, used for gentle exfoliation by people whose skin reacts to glycolic acid. Small trials suggest it irritates less than glycolic acid while improving texture; the evidence base is limited.

pha-polyhydroxy-acid.text: PHAs, mainly gluconolactone and lactobionic acid, are promoted as gentler cousins of AHAs for smoother, brighter skin, including skin that stings easily. The category is largely a marketing and chemical grouping, with sparse published trial data.

chain: Mild exfoliation and clearing of pores
willow-bark-extract.text: Willow bark extract is used in skincare as a natural source of salicin, marketed as a gentler salicylic-acid-like ingredient for clearer, smoother skin. Oral trials exist for back and joint pain; skin-specific trials have not been found.

birch-sap.text: Birch sap is a traditional tonic and hair or freckle wash that now appears in K-beauty serums for hydration and a fresher complexion. Skin evidence is mostly laboratory-level, with little human trial data.

erythromycin-topical.text: Topical erythromycin is a long-standing prescription treatment for acne, used to reduce acne bacteria and inflamed spots for clearer skin. Acne is its labelled use, and reviews list it alongside clindamycin among common topical antimicrobials.

minocycline-foam.text: Minocycline foam is a prescription topical antibiotic used for clearer skin in acne and reduced bumps and redness in rosacea. A 4% foam was studied for acne and a 1.5% foam for rosacea in Phase 3 trials.

ivermectin-cream.text: Ivermectin cream is a prescription treatment used to reduce the red bumps of papulopustular rosacea for a calmer-looking face. It is approved for this use and backed by Phase 3 trials.

quassia-amara-extract.text: A 4% quassia gel has been tried for rosacea and facial seborrheic dermatitis, aimed at reducing visible redness and flaking. Two small studies have examined it; larger trials have not been reported.

cimetidine-for-acne.text: Cimetidine, a stomach-acid drug, was tried off-label for acne decades ago because of its weak antiandrogen activity, by mouth and as a lotion. Supporting evidence for this acne use is limited.

chlormadinone-acetate-pill.text: Combined pills containing chlormadinone acetate, sold in places like Germany and Brazil, are used in some countries for androgen-related acne and excess hair. Acne is an off-label or regional use, and little acne-specific trial data has been found.

drospirenone-pill.text: Drospirenone combined pills such as Yasmin and Yaz are indicated for moderate acne in some regions, used for clearer skin through their antiandrogen action. Much of the published research focuses on PCOS.

ruxolitinib-cream.text: Ruxolitinib cream is a prescription JAK-inhibitor approved for vitiligo repigmentation and for atopic dermatitis, used to even out patchy skin tone. Phase 3 trials support both approvals.

tapinarof.text: Tapinarof is a prescription cream used to clear visible plaques in psoriasis and eczema. It is labelled for those conditions with phase 3 support; its use for seborrheic dermatitis has not been backed by trials found.

roflumilast-cream.text: Roflumilast cream and foam are prescription products approved for psoriasis, eczema and scalp or facial seborrheic dermatitis, used to clear visible redness and flaking. Phase 3 data support its psoriasis and eczema use.

chain: Dry shirts, no visible sweat marks
sofpironium.text: Sofpironium is a prescription underarm gel for excessive sweating, used to keep clothing dry and free of visible sweat marks. It is trial-backed for hyperhidrosis and approved in Japan as Ecclock; it is a medical treatment rather than a cosmetic.

dexpanthenol.text: Dexpanthenol is a barrier-supporting, soothing ingredient in skincare used for hydrated, calmer-looking skin. It has been studied mainly for wound healing and skin irritation rather than appearance outcomes.

calendula-extract.text: Calendula extract appears in soothing skincare for calmer-looking, less irritated skin. Studies have looked at wound healing, and no appearance-specific trials have been found.

ciclopirox-shampoo.text: Ciclopirox shampoo is a prescription antifungal wash used to clear scalp flaking and redness from seborrheic dermatitis. Several vehicle-controlled trials support that use; none have examined hair growth.

climbazole.text: Climbazole is an antifungal found in anti-dandruff shampoos and conditioners, used to reduce visible flaking. It belongs to the same class as ketoconazole; research in the sources is mostly environmental, with little clinical data cited.

coal-tar-shampoo.text: Coal tar shampoo is an old-school over-the-counter wash used to clear dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis and scalp psoriasis flakes. Trials support its effect on scalp flaking; it stains and smells strongly, which limits acceptance.

glycerin.text: Glycerin is a common moisturizer, cleanser and shaving ingredient used to keep skin hydrated and soft-looking. Its long use is well documented; cosmetic trials of glycerin itself were not found in the sources reviewed.

chain: Smoother, less chapped lips and skin
lanolin.text: Lanolin is an emollient wax used in lip balms and moisturizers to soften dry, chapped skin and lips. It resembles lipids in human skin; trials have focused mainly on sore nipples rather than facial appearance.
